Hatchlings of Archaeopteryx lithographica emerged from parchment-shelled eggs after a period of yolk-dependent embryonic development, and the wet weight at birth has been estimated from skeletal correlates at approximately 30 grams [Wwb = approximately 30 grams]. This modest neonatal mass, combined with the presumably altricial state of the hatchlings, suggests a growth trajectory that would ultimately culminate in a much larger adult size. The initial wet weight of the embryo at the onset of organogenesis, extrapolated from extant archosaurian developmental series, is placed at 39.6 grams [Ww0 = 39.6 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk investment typical of basal paravians. The leathery-shelled eggs of this species were likely incubated through a combination of maternal brooding and environmental heat, given the absence of evidence for advanced endothermy. Growth increments derived from femoral histology indicate that the maximum recorded adult body mass attained by this species reaches approximately 900 grams [Wwi = approximately 900 grams], a value consistent with estimates from the largest known specimens of the Solnhofen Limestone. This considerable increase in body mass from the hatchling stage to adulthood implies a prolonged period of somatic growth, with bone deposition rates that varied seasonally in response to resource availability in the Late Jurassic subtropical archipelago.

Sexual maturation in Archaeopteryx lithographica, inferred from the transition from rapidly deposited fibrolamellar bone to slower, more organized parallel-fibered bone in the cortex of the femur, occurred at a specific interval after the individual emerged from the egg. Under the thermal conditions typical of active physiological processes in this basal avialan, assumed to be near 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at approximately 2.5 years [tp = approximately 2.5 years]. This relatively rapid onset of reproductive capacity, when compared to the overall lifespan, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritized early breeding opportunities in a seasonally productive environment. The onset of gonadal activation would have coincided with the achievement of near-adult body dimensions, as the energetic demands of gametogenesis and subsequent nesting activity could only be sustained once the skeletal framework was largely complete. The attainment of sexual maturity marks a critical physiological threshold, after which resources were progressively diverted from somatic growth toward the production of yolk-laden eggs and the establishment of breeding territories.

The maximum recorded longevity of Archaeopteryx lithographica, derived from counts of arrested growth lines in the periosteal cortices of long bones, has been estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. When evaluated against the metabolic regime presumed for this species, operating at an internal body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], this lifespan aligns with the lower end of the range observed in extant, similarly sized ground-foraging birds such as the Eurasian jay. The presence of multiple closely spaced lines of arrested growth in several specimens suggests that individuals regularly experienced periods of physiological stress, likely linked to seasonal resource bottlenecks or the energetic costs of reproduction, which may have truncated the potential lifespan of some individuals. Despite these challenges, the skeletal evidence indicates that a portion of the population successfully reached this advanced age, allowing for multiple reproductive seasons over the course of a lifetime. This longevity, combined with the relatively early age at puberty, implies that a reproductively active adult could contribute offspring to the population for several consecutive years, buffering against years of poor fledging success.

Reproductive output in Archaeopteryx lithographica remains a topic of considerable speculation due to the scarcity of direct fossil evidence for clutch size and nesting frequency. Based on comparisons with extant ground-nesting birds and non-avian maniraptoran dinosaurs, it is hypothesized that females laid approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year]. Each clutch likely contained between 4 and 6 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch likely contained between 4 and 6 eggs], a range inferred from the number of eggs preserved in association with adult skeletons of closely related paravians from the same lithographic limestones. This level of annual reproductive effort, when compared to the relatively high ultimate wet weight of 900 grams [Wwi = 900 grams], suggests a reproductive strategy that prioritized investment in relatively few, well-provisioned offspring over the production of large numbers of smaller eggs. The substantial yolk content of each egg would have provided the developing embryo with sufficient nutrients to hatch at a relatively advanced stage of development, potentially reducing the duration of the most vulnerable early postnatal period.

The combined reproductive and life-history traits of Archaeopteryx lithographica paint a picture of a moderately long-lived, slow-breeding species that was constrained by the energetic realities of its placodontivorous or insectivorous diet in a seasonally arid subtropical habitat.
